newsitem.title: NAMIBIA: Investors ignore Southern Africa reform efforts.
newsitem.headline: Investors ignore Southern Africa reform efforts.

text.p: Investors have largely ignored the efforts to liberalise the economies of the 12-member Southern African Development Community (SADC), officials said on Wednesday.
Now the trade group, struggling for a place in the global market, is looking beyond the recipes of the World Bank and International Monetary Fund (IMF) for improvement.

"Most SADC member states have implemented policies which according to the World Bank and the IMF are necessary for the positive contribution of foreign investment to economic development of the SADC countries," said Phakamani Radebe, Deputy Director of SADC's Finance and Investment Sector Coordination Unit (FISCU).

"What we have now learned is that although liberalising our economies is essential, in itself it is not sufficient, and SADC countries need to build domestic and regional productive capacity as the basis for their own long-term development," he added.
Radebe believes SADC needs to find out why the desired level of direct foreign investment has not been achieved.

Fresh from preliminary discussions in advance of the 1997 SADC consultative conference, being held in the Namibian capital Windhoek, Radebe said most regional economies still suffered from lack of basic infrastructure and from a narrow production base.
"The current environment in the SADC region is too weak to guarantee that the region will benefit from globalisation", he said.
This year's conference, which formally starts on Thursday, will put a special emphasis on improving productivity.
"Productivity levels and trends will be crucial in attracting foreign investment and enhancing the competitive edge of southern African companies", SADC Executive Secretary Kaire Mbuende said.
SADC's finance and investment sector has conducted three studies to help lay the foundation for further development in the region.

These include a study of macroeconomic policies in the region, the possibility of a regional bank or financial mechanism to close the funding gap when donor money dries up, and the promotion of investment in the region.
Radebe said a study on the setting up of a regional bank would be completed in June.
Abraham Pallanayo, director of SADC's trade and industry sector said the region also needed to expand trade among its own members as well as cross border investment.
He said although the volume of trade among member countries had improved since South Africa joined SADC, more was needed towards establishing a free trade area within eight years.
SADC countries signed a trade protocol last year which is aimed at establishing a regional free trade area in the next eight years.
SADC comprises Mauritius, Angola, Lesotho, Swaziland, Zambia, Zimbabwe, Namibia, Mozambique, Tanzania, Malawi, South Africa and Botswana.
